summary:
ORBIT-M is a prototype decision-support tool for spacewalk (EVA) readiness, built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Haifa. We developed an interactive dashboard that brings together each astronaut's sleep, reaction time, symptoms, vision, vital signs, recovery after earlier EVAs, and radiation and suit conditions. It compares them with that person's own baseline and the planned EVA duration. It then shows a plain GREEN, YELLOW or RED status, with the reasons and the source behind every rule.
NASA still lists EVA preparedness shortly after landing on a planetary surface as an open research gap. We address it by judging each astronaut against their own baseline instead of population averages. It runs onboard first and sends a summary to Earth in parallel, so it stays useful during communication delays of 20 minutes or more.
This matters because future crews on the Moon or Mars may need to perform EVAs with no rescue team nearby and slow contact with Earth. ORBIT-M supports, and never replaces, flight-surgeon clearance. Our demo uses synthetic data and cutoffs modeled on NASA sources.
details:
We are ORBIT-M, and this is our pitch for our project for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Haifa. It’s a prototype decision-support tool that helps a crew see whether an astronaut’s current condition fits a planned or emergency spacewalk (EVA). Ground medical clearance already exists before each planned EVA, but not before emergency ones, and we don’t aim to replace it. We focus on the time just before the EVA. We compare each person’s measurements (sleep, reaction time, symptoms, vision, vital signs, recovery after earlier EVAs, and radiation and suit conditions) with that person’s own baseline, and we take the planned EVA duration into account. The tool then shows a plain status: GREEN means no concern found, YELLOW means review first, and RED means stop and apply the approved procedure. Every status comes with its reasons and the source behind each rule. It runs onboard first and sends a summary to Earth in parallel, so it stays useful during communication delays of 20 minutes or more.

Our interactive demo uses fictional astronauts and synthetic data modeled on NASA sources. We label our numerical cutoffs as unvalidated demonstration rules, and we don’t present them as NASA thresholds. As next steps, we would compare the flags with flight-surgeon decisions, calibrate with task-performance data such as NASA’s CIPHER and Mini FTT, test with analog crews, and have specialists approve any operational threshold.
